extracted.intended_audience: general readers, historians, archivists, legal scholars, students researching presidential records and executive orders
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of Executive Order 13233 (2001) describing its provisions limiting access to former Presidents' records, the legal and legislative background, criticisms, lawsuits, and its eventual revocation. Useful for readers seeking the rules and controversies around access to presidential records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential Records Act (1978) — public availability timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: The Presidential Records Act of 1978 mandated that the records of former presidents would automatically become the property of the federal government upon their departures from the Oval Office, and then transferred to the Archivist of the United States, thereafter to be made available to the public after no more than 12 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the baseline statutory rule for custody and public access timing for presidential records; EO13233 and related actions operate in relation to this 12-year availability presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential Recordings and Materials Preservation Act (1974) — federal custody to prevent destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress passed the Presidential Recordings and Materials Preservation Act of 1974, placing the presidential records of Richard Nixon in federal custody to prevent their destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical statutory precedent showing congressional intent to preserve presidential records and reduce secrecy; provides context for later PRA (1978) protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 2(b) of Executive Order 12667 — Archivist delay at incumbent President's instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2(b) of Executive Order 12667 requires the Archivist of the United States to delay release of Presidential records at the instruction of the current President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under EO12667 the incumbent President could instruct the Archivist to delay release; EO13233 revoked EO12667's Section 13 and altered the balance between incumbent and former Presidents' review rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of records restricted by Executive Order 13233
rubrics_metrics.description: EO13233 limited access to records "...reflecting military, diplomatic, or national security secrets, Presidential communications, legal advice, legal work, or the deliberative processes of the President and the President's advisers..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EO13233 broadened the types of material that could be withheld or subjected to review; the Order referenced adherence to Supreme Court decisions such as Nixon v. Administrator of General Services in applying these exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former President review period under §3(b) of EO13233
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(b) of EO13233: "After receiving the records he requests, the former President shall review those records as expeditiously as possible, and for no longer than 90 days for requests that are not unduly burdensome. The Archivist shall not permit access to the records by a requester during this period of review or when requested by the former President to extend the time for review."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gave former Presidents an explicit review period (up to 90 days for non- unduly burdensome requests) during which the Archivist must withhold access; courts later scrutinized and limited reliance on this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review and APA ruling against Archivist reliance on §3(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: In October 2007 the Court held that "the Archivist’s reliance on § 3(b) of Executive Order 13,233 is arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and not in accordance with law in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act" and enjoined the Archivist from further relying on §3(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court disapproved the Archivist's application of the former President review provision as implemented; most of the lawsuit was otherwise dismissed as not ripe at that time and the rest dismissed without prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation by Executive Order 13489 and restoration of prior wording
rubrics_metrics.description: On January 21, 2009, Executive Order 13233 was revoked by President Barack Obama (EO13489), which essentially restored most of the wording of EO12667 with some modifications; one notable change named vice presidential records as explicitly covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EO13489 nullified EO13233 and re-established the earlier framework (EO12667) with minor changes, reducing the access-limiting provisions introduced by EO13233.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative attempts to void or amend EO13233 (H.R.1255, H.R.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple bills (e.g., H.R.1255, Presidential Records Act Amendments of 2007; H.R.35 in the 111th Congress) were introduced to negate or amend EO13233 and restore or clarify access rules; some passed committees or the House but ultimately died in the Senate or lapsed with the end of a Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congressional action repeatedly sought to limit or reverse EO13233's effects; legislative history shows political and institutional opposition to EO13233 from archivists, historians, and library associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism from professional organizations regarding EO13233's conformity with 44 U.S.C. §§ 2201–2207
rubrics_metrics.description: The Society of American Archivists and the American Library Association claimed EO13233 "violates both the spirit and letter of existing U.S. law on access to presidential papers as clearly laid down in 44 U.S.C. §§ 2201–2207," arguing the order threatens to undermine public access to presidential papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects professional-standards-based objections that EO13233 conflicted with statutory goals of the PRA and scholarly access; used as part of public and legislative arguments against the Order.
